WORKERS' COMPENSATION CLAIM NOTICE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

INJURY AND CLAIM INFORMATION DECLARATION
I, Jordan Lee, am completing this information sheet in connection with a work injury I sustained while employed by Acme, Inc. The injury is described here as: lower back strain from lifting, occurring on October 1, 2026. Written notice of the injury was given to Acme, Inc. on October 2, 2026.

This information sheet describes California's statutory framework governing an employee's duty to notify an employer of a work injury, an employer's duty to provide a claim form, the timing for the claim to be accepted or rejected, the deadline to file a workers' compensation claim, and the general rule that workers' compensation is an employee's exclusive remedy against the employer, subject to specific statutory exceptions.

This information sheet is not a workers' compensation claim form, is not itself filed with any employer, insurer, or agency by completing it, and does not initiate a workers' compensation claim. Completing it does not determine that Jordan Lee's injury is compensable, and does not determine the outcome of any claim. Only the employer's claims administrator, the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board, or a court on review can determine whether a specific injury is compensable.

DUTY TO NOTIFY EMPLOYER OF INJURY
California Labor Code § 5400 — not § 5401 — is the section that states the employee's notice duty: except as provided by §§ 5402 and 5403, no claim to recover workers' compensation may be maintained unless, within thirty days after the injury occurs, written notice signed by the injured person (or, if the person has died, by a dependent) is served on the employer. Section 5401 is a different duty running the other way — it requires the employer, not the employee, to hand over a claim form once the employer has notice or knowledge of the injury, and is addressed in a separate clause of this document. Section 5403 qualifies § 5400's thirty-day rule: a failure to give notice, or a defect or inaccuracy in the notice that was given, is not a bar to recovery if it is found as a fact that the employer was not in fact misled or prejudiced by the failure or defect.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "no claim to recover compensation under this division shall be maintained unless within thirty days after the occurrence of the injury which is claimed to have caused the disability or death, there is served upon the employer notice in writing, signed by the person injured or someone in his behalf"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 5400 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 5400 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=5400.)
  "The failure to give notice under section 5400, or any defect or inaccuracy in a notice is not a bar to recovery under this division if it is found as a fact in the proceedings for the collection of the claim that the employer was not in fact misled or prejudiced by such failure."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 5403 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 5403 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=5403.)
  Known gap: Correcting the framing in the research request: § 5400 itself is the source of the thirty-day notice duty, and it is § 5400 — not § 5401 — that states it; § 5401 imposes a distinct, employer-side duty (the claim-form and notice-of-eligibility duty), addressed in a separate clause. Section 5403's exception is also narrower than a general "good cause for late notice" standard: it does not ask whether the employee had a good excuse for being late, but only whether the employer was in fact misled or prejudiced by the missing or defective notice — an employer who was not misled or prejudiced cannot defeat the claim on notice grounds even without any excuse for the delay, and an employer who was misled or prejudiced might still defeat it even if the employee had a good excuse. A third, related exception — that an employer's own actual knowledge of the injury from any source is equivalent to notice under § 5400 — is stated in § 5402(a) and is addressed in a separate clause of this document rather than repeated here; §§ 5400, 5402, and 5403 are three separate sections of the same statutory chapter (Chapter 2, Limitations of Proceedings), not independent sources from one another, and this disclosure is repeated in each clause that draws on that chapter. This clause is one state's statute, stating a fact about California's notice requirement — not a claim about what any specific reader with a specific injury should do about giving or not giving notice.

EMPLOYER'S ACTUAL KNOWLEDGE AS EQUIVALENT TO NOTICE
California Labor Code § 5402(a) states that knowledge of an injury, obtained from any source, on the part of the employer, the employer's managing agent, superintendent, foreman, or other person in authority — or knowledge that a claim of injury is being asserted, sufficient to give the employer an opportunity to investigate — is equivalent to the written notice that § 5400 otherwise requires the employee to serve on the employer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Knowledge of an injury, obtained from any source, on the part of an employer, the employer’s managing agent, superintendent, foreman, or other person in authority, or knowledge of the assertion of a claim of injury sufficient to afford opportunity to the employer to make an investigation into the facts, is equivalent to service under Section 5400."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 5402(a) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 5402, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=5402.)
  Known gap: This is a fact about what satisfies the notice requirement, not a claim about whether any specific employer in fact had the relevant knowledge in any given case — that is a factual question this document does not resolve. Section 5402 also contains, in separate subdivisions (b) and (c), the claim-response and treatment-authorization rules addressed in a different clause of this document ("Time Limit to Reject the Claim; Presumption of Compensability"); this clause and that one draw on different subdivisions of the same statutory section, so they are not independent sources of each other, and this disclosure is repeated in the other clause.

EMPLOYER'S DUTY TO PROVIDE THE CLAIM FORM
California Labor Code § 5401(a) requires the employer, within one working day of receiving notice or knowledge of an injury that causes lost time beyond the employee's work shift or requires medical treatment beyond first aid, to provide the injured employee (or, in case of death, the dependents) a claim form and a notice of potential eligibility for benefits, personally or by first-class mail. The claim form itself must request the employee's name and address, social security number, the time and address where the injury occurred, and the nature of and body part affected by the injury. Section 5401(b) further requires that the notice of potential eligibility, insofar as practicable combined with the claim form into a single document, be easily understandable, available in English and Spanish, and cover specified topics — including the claims procedure, the types of benefits available, how to obtain medical care while the claim is pending, and the employee's right to consult an attorney.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Within one working day of receiving notice or knowledge of injury under Section 5400 or 5402, which injury results in lost time beyond the employee’s work shift at the time of injury or which results in medical treatment beyond first aid, the employer shall provide, personally or by first-class mail, a claim form and a notice of potential eligibility for benefits under this division to the injured employee"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 5401(a) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 5401, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=5401.)
  "The claim form shall request the injured employee’s name and address, social security number, the time and address where the injury occurred, and the nature of and part of the body affected by the injury."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 5401(a) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 5401, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=5401.)
  Known gap: The claim form § 5401 describes is commonly referred to in practice as form "DWC-1," but that name and number do not themselves appear anywhere in the text of § 5401 — the statute only calls it "a claim form." This document did not independently fetch or verify the regulation that assigns that form its title and number, so no citation or quote is offered for the "DWC-1" label itself; it is stated here only as commonly-used shorthand for the form § 5401 describes, not as a verified statutory fact. This clause is one state's statute, stating a fact about what California requires an employer to provide and when — not a claim about whether any specific employer has done so in any given case.

TIME LIMIT TO REJECT THE CLAIM; PRESUMPTION OF COMPENSABILITY
California Labor Code § 5402(b)(1) states that if liability is not rejected within 90 days after the date the claim form is filed under § 5401, the injury is presumed compensable — a presumption rebuttable only by evidence discovered after that 90-day period. (§ 5402(b)(2) sets a shorter 75-day version of that same presumption for certain injuries or illnesses defined elsewhere in the Labor Code, at §§ 3212 through 3212.85 and 3212.9 through 3213.2.) Separately, § 5402(c) requires the employer, within one working day after the employee files the claim form, to authorize treatment for the alleged injury and continue providing it until liability is accepted or rejected — with the employer's liability for that pre-decision treatment capped at $10,000 while the claim remains undecided.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If liability is not rejected within 90 days after the date the claim form is filed under Section 5401, the injury shall be presumed compensable under this division. The presumption of this subdivision is rebuttable only by evidence discovered subsequent to the 90-day period."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 5402(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 5402, subd. (b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=5402.)
  "Within one working day after an employee files a claim form under Section 5401, the employer shall authorize the provision of all treatment, consistent with Section 5307.27, for the alleged injury and shall continue to provide the treatment until the date that liability for the claim is accepted or rejected. Until the date the claim is accepted or rejected, liability for medical treatment shall be limited to ten thousand dollars ($10,000)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 5402(c) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 5402, subd. (c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=5402.)
  Known gap: Correcting the framing in the research request: the statutory text of § 5402 does not itself contain, describe, or use the term "delay letter" anywhere in its current form. A "delay letter" is a term used in workers' compensation administrative practice for correspondence a claims administrator sends to extend its investigation, but no provision of § 5402 was found stating a right or procedure by that name, and this document does not independently verify against the applicable regulations (outside the Labor Code itself) whether or how such a letter affects the 90-day or 75-day period stated here. That specific mechanism is therefore omitted from this clause rather than asserted without a verified source. The 75-day presumption for the injury categories cross-referenced in § 5402(b)(2) is stated here only by cross-reference; this document does not independently identify or verify what those injury categories are. This clause is one state's statute, used as evidence of the actual statutory timing — not a claim about whether any specific claim was or was not timely rejected.

TIME LIMIT TO FILE A WORKERS' COMPENSATION CLAIM
California Labor Code § 5405 sets a one-year period to commence proceedings to collect medical-treatment benefits or disability-payment benefits, running from any of three alternative dates: the date of injury; the expiration of any period covered by disability payments; or the last date on which medical benefits were furnished — whichever produces the latest date is, as a practical matter, the one that governs, since the statute states these as three independent starting points rather than requiring all three. Separately, § 5401(d) provides that once a claim form is filed with the employer, that filing tolls (pauses) the running of this time limit — for injuries occurring on or after January 1, 1994 — until the claim is either denied by the employer or becomes presumptively compensable under § 5402.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The period within which proceedings may be commenced for the collection of the benefits provided by Article 2 (commencing with Section 4600) or Article 3 (commencing with Section 4650), or both, of Chapter 2 of Part 2 is one year from any of the following: (a) The date of injury. (b) The expiration of any period covered by payment under Article 3 (commencing with Section 4650) of Chapter 2 of Part 2. (c) The last date on which any benefits provided for in Article 2 (commencing with Section 4600) of Chapter 2 of Part 2 were furnished."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 5405 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 5405 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=5405.)
  "Filing of the claim form with the employer shall toll, for injuries occurring on or after January 1, 1994, the time limitations set forth in Sections 5405 and 5406 until the claim is denied by the employer or the injury becomes presumptively compensable pursuant to Section 5402."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 5401(d) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 5401, subd. (d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=5401.)
  Known gap: Correcting the framing in the research request: § 5405's one-year period does not run from the date of injury alone — the statute states three independent alternative trigger dates, and the last-furnished-benefits or last-payment dates can extend the effective deadline well past one year from the injury itself where treatment or disability payments continued. This document does not resolve, for any specific case, which of the three dates produces the applicable deadline, nor does it independently verify what benefits were or were not furnished in a specific case. The tolling rule in § 5401(d) is stated by its own terms to apply to injuries occurring on or after January 1, 1994; this document does not evaluate whether that date restriction is a live limitation for any specific injury. Sections 5401 and 5405 are two separate sections of the same statutory chapter, not independent sources from each other.

WORKERS' COMPENSATION AS THE EXCLUSIVE REMEDY
California Labor Code § 3600(a) makes an employer liable for workers' compensation, without regard to negligence, whenever specified conditions concur — including that the injury arose out of and in the course of employment. Labor Code § 3602(a) then states the exclusivity consequence: where § 3600's conditions of compensation concur, the right to recover workers' compensation is, except as specifically provided in § 3602 itself and in §§ 3706 and 4558, the sole and exclusive remedy of the employee (or dependents) against the employer — meaning a separate civil lawsuit against the employer for the same injury is generally unavailable. Section 3602(a) also states that an employer's occupying some other or "dual" capacity besides employer does not, by itself, open the door to a civil damages action.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Liability for the compensation provided by this division, in lieu of any other liability whatsoever to any person except as otherwise specifically provided in Sections 3602, 3706, and 4558, shall, without regard to negligence, exist against an employer for any injury sustained by his or her employees arising out of and in the course of the employment and for the death of any employee if the injury proximately causes death"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 3600(a) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 3600, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=3600.)
  "Where the conditions of compensation set forth in Section 3600 concur, the right to recover compensation is, except as specifically provided in this section and Sections 3706 and 4558, the sole and exclusive remedy of the employee or his or her dependents against the employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 3602(a) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 3602, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=3602.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general rule only; the named, specific exceptions to it — including the ones § 3602(a) itself cross-references — are addressed in a separate clause of this document rather than repeated here, so this clause should not be read in isolation as stating an absolute bar. Sections 3600 and 3602 are two separate sections of the same statutory chapter (Chapter 3, Conditions of Compensation Liability), not independent sources from each other. Two further cross-referenced exceptions — Labor Code § 3706 (concerning uninsured employers) and § 4558 (concerning power-press injuries) — are named in both § 3600(a) and § 3602(a) but were not independently fetched or verified in this session, so this document does not state or quote what either of those sections provides; a reader would need to separately check those two sections' actual text, which this document does not do. This clause is one state's statute, stating a fact about the general scope of California's exclusive-remedy rule — not a claim about whether workers' compensation is in fact the exclusive remedy for any specific injury or any specific reader's situation.

STATUTORY EXCEPTIONS TO THE EXCLUSIVE REMEDY RULE
California Labor Code § 3602(b) names specific, narrow instances in which an employee (or dependents, if the employee dies) may bring a civil damages action against the employer despite § 3602(a)'s general exclusivity rule: (1) where the injury or death is proximately caused by a willful physical assault by the employer; (2) where the injury is aggravated by the employer's fraudulent concealment of the existence of the injury and its connection to the employment — in which case the employer's civil liability is limited to the damages proximately caused by that aggravation, and the employer bears the burden of proving how much of the harm to apportion away from it; and (3) where the injury or death is proximately caused by a defective product the employer manufactured and then sold, leased, or otherwise transferred for value to an independent third person, who in turn provided it for the employee's use.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employee, or his or her dependents in the event of his or her death, may bring an action at law for damages against the employer, as if this division did not apply, in the following instances: (1) Where the employee’s injury or death is proximately caused by a willful physical assault by the employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 3602(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 3602, subd. (b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=3602.)
  "Where the employee’s injury is aggravated by the employer’s fraudulent concealment of the existence of the injury and its connection with the employment, in which case the employer’s liability shall be limited to those damages proximately caused by the aggravation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 3602(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 3602, subd. (b)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=3602.)
  Known gap: Correcting the framing in the research request: California's statutory exceptions to exclusivity are not a general "intentional torts" carve-out — § 3602(b) names three specific, narrowly worded instances (willful physical assault by the employer; fraudulent concealment of an existing injury; and a defective-product chain involving a third party), not intentional wrongdoing by the employer generally. Whether a given intentional act by an employer falls within the willful-physical-assault exception specifically, as opposed to being barred by exclusivity like other workplace torts, is a fact-specific application question this document does not resolve, and this document does not independently research case law construing the scope of that exception's terms. This clause quotes § 3602(b)(1) and (b)(2); § 3602(b)(3) (the defective-product exception) is described but not separately quoted here. Section 3602 is the same section already quoted (subdivision (a)) in a separate clause of this document addressing the general exclusivity rule; that clause and this one draw on the same statutory section, not independent sources of each other.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — WORKERS' COMPENSATION CLAIM NOTICE INFORMATION SHEET
I declare that the information above is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on October 3, 2026 at San Francisco, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes the statutory framework governing notice of a work injury, the claim form process, the timing for a claims administrator to accept or reject a claim, the deadline to file a workers' compensation claim, and the exclusive-remedy rule, as set out in the California Labor Code. It is not a workers' compensation claim form, is not filed with any employer, insurer, or agency by completing it, does not itself determine that Jordan Lee has a compensable injury or that Acme, Inc. owes any benefit, is not a substitute for the actual claim form or the statutes and regulations governing the workers' compensation claims process, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.]

expectedJSON.body: California Labor Code § 3600(a) makes an employer liable for workers' compensation, without regard to negligence, whenever specified conditions concur — including that the injury arose out of and in the course of employment. Labor Code § 3602(a) then states the exclusivity consequence: where § 3600's conditions of compensation concur, the right to recover workers' compensation is, except as specifically provided in § 3602 itself and in §§ 3706 and 4558, the sole and exclusive remedy of the employee (or dependents) against the employer — meaning a separate civil lawsuit against the employer for the same injury is generally unavailable. Section 3602(a) also states that an employer's occupying some other or "dual" capacity besides employer does not, by itself, open the door to a civil damages action.

citations.quote: Where the conditions of compensation set forth in Section 3600 concur, the right to recover compensation is, except as specifically provided in this section and Sections 3706 and 4558, the sole and exclusive remedy of the employee or his or her dependents against the employer.

Sections 3600 and 3602 are two separate sections of the same statutory chapter (Chapter 3, Conditions of Compensation Liability), not independent sources from each other. Two further cross-referenced exceptions — Labor Code § 3706 (concerning uninsured employers) and § 4558 (concerning power-press injuries) — are named in both § 3600(a) and § 3602(a) but were not independently fetched or verified in this session, so this document does not state or quote what either of those sections provides; a reader would need to separately check those two sections' actual text, which this document does not do. This clause is one state's statute, stating a fact about the general scope of California's exclusive-remedy rule — not a claim about whether workers' compensation is in fact the exclusive remedy for any specific injury or any specific reader's situation.

expectedJSON.body: California Labor Code § 3602(b) names specific, narrow instances in which an employee (or dependents, if the employee dies) may bring a civil damages action against the employer despite § 3602(a)'s general exclusivity rule: (1) where the injury or death is proximately caused by a willful physical assault by the employer; (2) where the injury is aggravated by the employer's fraudulent concealment of the existence of the injury and its connection to the employment — in which case the employer's civil liability is limited to the damages proximately caused by that aggravation, and the employer bears the burden of proving how much of the harm to apportion away from it; and (3) where the injury or death is proximately caused by a defective product the employer manufactured and then sold, leased, or otherwise transferred for value to an independent third person, who in turn provided it for the employee's use.

citations.quote: An employee, or his or her dependents in the event of his or her death, may bring an action at law for damages against the employer, as if this division did not apply, in the following instances: (1) Where the employee’s injury or death is proximately caused by a willful physical assault by the employer.

citations.quote: Where the employee’s injury is aggravated by the employer’s fraudulent concealment of the existence of the injury and its connection with the employment, in which case the employer’s liability shall be limited to those damages proximately caused by the aggravation.

Whether a given intentional act by an employer falls within the willful-physical-assault exception specifically, as opposed to being barred by exclusivity like other workplace torts, is a fact-specific application question this document does not resolve, and this document does not independently research case law construing the scope of that exception's terms.
